title: Statistical Mechanics
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Statistical Mechanics curriculum: thermodynamics review (state functions, entropy), microstates/macrostates and equal a priori probabilities, statistical ensembles (microcanonical and canonical), the Boltzmann distribution and partition function, connecting the partition function to thermodynamic quantities, the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution, quantum statistics (Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac, contrasted with classical statistics), and applications including the ideal gas law, specific heat of solids, and blackbody radiation.

questions.question: In thermodynamics, a 'state function' is a quantity that
options: Depends only on the current equilibrium state of the system, not on the path taken to reach it
Depends only on the process or path by which the system reached its current state
Is always conserved during any thermodynamic process
Can only be defined for reversible processes
questions.correct_answer: Depends only on the current equilibrium state of the system, not on the path taken to reach it
questions.explanation: State functions such as internal energy, entropy, and temperature are properties of the equilibrium state itself; unlike heat and work, their change between two states is independent of the process connecting them.

questions.question: The thermodynamic entropy S of a system, in the framework connected to statistical mechanics, is fundamentally a measure of
options: The number of microscopic configurations (microstates) consistent with the system's macroscopic state
The total kinetic energy of all particles in the system
The temperature of the system alone
The pressure exerted by the system on its container
questions.correct_answer: The number of microscopic configurations (microstates) consistent with the system's macroscopic state
questions.explanation: Statistical mechanics gives entropy a microscopic meaning: it quantifies the multiplicity of accessible microstates, connecting thermodynamic disorder to statistical counting.

questions.question: A 'microstate' of a system refers to
options: A complete, detailed specification of the state of every individual particle in the system (e.g., position and momentum of each particle)
A macroscopic description using only pressure, volume, and temperature
The state of the system after it has been observed and collapsed
A state defined only for solids, not gases
questions.correct_answer: A complete, detailed specification of the state of every individual particle in the system (e.g., position and momentum of each particle)
questions.explanation: Microstates specify the exact configuration of every constituent particle, in contrast to macrostates which are characterized by a small number of bulk (macroscopic) variables.

questions.question: A 'macrostate' is characterized by
options: A small set of bulk thermodynamic variables such as total energy, volume, pressure, and temperature
The exact position and velocity of every particle in the system
A single microstate only
The quantum state of an individual particle
questions.correct_answer: A small set of bulk thermodynamic variables such as total energy, volume, pressure, and temperature
questions.explanation: Macrostates describe the system at the level accessible to macroscopic measurement, and typically correspond to an enormous number of possible underlying microstates.

questions.question: The postulate of equal a priori probabilities in statistical mechanics states that
options: For an isolated system in equilibrium, all accessible microstates consistent with the given macroscopic constraints are equally likely
Only the microstate of lowest energy is ever occupied
Microstates with higher energy are always more probable than those with lower energy
Probability only applies to quantum systems, not classical ones
questions.correct_answer: For an isolated system in equilibrium, all accessible microstates consistent with the given macroscopic constraints are equally likely
questions.explanation: This is the foundational postulate of statistical mechanics: in the absence of any other information, an isolated system in equilibrium is assumed to be found with equal probability in any of its accessible microstates.
questions.topic: Postulate of equal a priori probabilities

questions.question: The Boltzmann entropy formula relating entropy S to the number of accessible microstates Omega is
options: S = k_B * ln(Omega)
S = k_B * Omega
S = k_B / ln(Omega)
S = Omega / k_B
questions.correct_answer: S = k_B * ln(Omega)
questions.explanation: This is Boltzmann's famous formula, connecting the macroscopic thermodynamic entropy to the logarithm of the number of microstates Omega, with k_B the Boltzmann constant.

questions.question: The microcanonical ensemble in statistical mechanics describes a system that is
options: Isolated, with fixed total energy E, fixed volume V, and fixed particle number N
In thermal contact with a heat bath at fixed temperature T
Able to exchange both energy and particles with a reservoir
Always at zero temperature
questions.correct_answer: Isolated, with fixed total energy E, fixed volume V, and fixed particle number N
questions.explanation: The microcanonical ensemble models a completely isolated system (constant E, V, N), where all accessible microstates of that fixed energy are equally probable, consistent with the equal a priori probability postulate.

questions.question: The canonical ensemble in statistical mechanics describes a system that is
options: In thermal equilibrium with a large heat reservoir at fixed temperature T, allowed to exchange energy but not particles
Completely isolated with no energy exchange of any kind
Allowed to exchange both particles and energy with a reservoir
Restricted to only a single accessible microstate
questions.correct_answer: In thermal equilibrium with a large heat reservoir at fixed temperature T, allowed to exchange energy but not particles
questions.explanation: The canonical ensemble fixes N, V, and T (rather than E), representing a system in contact with a much larger heat bath, so its energy fluctuates but its temperature is well defined.

questions.question: In the canonical ensemble, the probability that a system is found in a particular microstate i with energy E_i is proportional to
options: exp(-E_i / (k_B*T))
exp(+E_i / (k_B*T))
E_i / (k_B*T)
1/E_i
questions.correct_answer: exp(-E_i / (k_B*T))
questions.explanation: This is the Boltzmann distribution: the probability of a microstate decreases exponentially with its energy, weighted by the thermal energy scale k_B*T.

questions.question: The canonical partition function Z is defined as
options: Z = sum over all microstates i of exp(-E_i/(k_B*T))
Z = sum over all microstates i of E_i
Z = the total number of microstates only, without any Boltzmann weighting
Z = k_B*T * ln(Omega)
questions.correct_answer: Z = sum over all microstates i of exp(-E_i/(k_B*T))
questions.explanation: The partition function is the normalization constant of the Boltzmann distribution, obtained by summing the Boltzmann factor over all accessible microstates; it encodes all the thermodynamic information of the system.

questions.question: The Helmholtz free energy F of a system is related to the canonical partition function Z by
options: F = -k_B*T*ln(Z)
F = k_B*T*Z
F = -k_B*ln(Z)/T
F = k_B*T/ln(Z)
questions.correct_answer: F = -k_B*T*ln(Z)
questions.explanation: This key relation allows all thermodynamic quantities to be derived from the partition function, since F is a natural thermodynamic potential for systems held at constant N, V, T.

questions.question: The average (internal) energy U of a system can be obtained from the partition function Z by the relation
options: U = -d(ln Z)/d(beta), where beta = 1/(k_B*T)
U = k_B*T*Z
U = ln(Z)
U = d(Z)/dT only, with no logarithm
questions.correct_answer: U = -d(ln Z)/d(beta), where beta = 1/(k_B*T)
questions.explanation: Differentiating the logarithm of the partition function with respect to beta = 1/(k_B T) yields the average energy, a standard derivation connecting statistical and thermodynamic descriptions.

questions.question: The entropy S can be obtained from the Helmholtz free energy F via the thermodynamic relation
options: S = -(dF/dT) at constant volume
S = F/T
S = dF/dV
S = -F*T
questions.correct_answer: S = -(dF/dT) at constant volume
questions.explanation: This is a standard thermodynamic identity (from dF = -SdT - PdV) that allows entropy to be computed once the free energy is known as a function of temperature from the partition function.

questions.question: The pressure P of a system can be derived from the Helmholtz free energy F using
options: P = -(dF/dV) at constant temperature
P = F*V
P = dF/dT
P = -F/V
questions.correct_answer: P = -(dF/dV) at constant temperature
questions.explanation: From the thermodynamic identity dF = -SdT - PdV, pressure is obtained as the negative volume derivative of the Helmholtz free energy at fixed temperature, linking the partition function directly to the equation of state.

questions.question: The Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution describes
options: The probability distribution of molecular speeds in a classical ideal gas at thermal equilibrium
The distribution of energy levels in a quantum harmonic oscillator
The distribution of electron spins in a magnetic field
The spatial distribution of photons in blackbody radiation only
questions.correct_answer: The probability distribution of molecular speeds in a classical ideal gas at thermal equilibrium
questions.explanation: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution gives the probability density for molecular speeds in an ideal gas, derived by combining the Boltzmann factor with the density of states in velocity space.

questions.question: In the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution, as temperature increases, the distribution of molecular speeds
options: Broadens and shifts to higher speeds, with the peak (most probable speed) moving to larger values
Narrows and shifts to lower speeds
Remains completely unchanged
Becomes a delta function at a single fixed speed
questions.correct_answer: Broadens and shifts to higher speeds, with the peak (most probable speed) moving to larger values
questions.explanation: Since the average kinetic energy scales with temperature, higher T increases both the mean speed and the spread of the speed distribution, flattening and shifting the curve rightward.

questions.question: The most probable speed v_p in the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution for a gas of molecular mass m at temperature T is given by
options: v_p = sqrt(2*k_B*T/m)
v_p = sqrt(3*k_B*T/m)
v_p = sqrt(8*k_B*T/(pi*m))
v_p = k_B*T/m
questions.correct_answer: v_p = sqrt(2*k_B*T/m)
questions.explanation: The most probable speed is found by maximizing the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution function, giving v_p = sqrt(2k_BT/m), which is smaller than both the average speed and the root-mean-square speed.

questions.question: For a Maxwell-Boltzmann gas at a given temperature, ranking the characteristic speeds from smallest to largest gives
options: Most probable speed < average speed < root-mean-square speed
Root-mean-square speed < average speed < most probable speed
Average speed < most probable speed < root-mean-square speed
All three speeds are always exactly equal
questions.correct_answer: Most probable speed < average speed < root-mean-square speed
questions.explanation: Because the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is asymmetric (skewed toward high speeds), the three characteristic speeds differ, with v_p < v_avg < v_rms, a standard and testable result.

questions.question: Bose-Einstein statistics applies to particles known as bosons, which have
options: Integer spin, and are not subject to the Pauli exclusion principle
Half-integer spin, and obey the Pauli exclusion principle
No spin under any circumstances
Only positive electric charge
questions.correct_answer: Integer spin, and are not subject to the Pauli exclusion principle
questions.explanation: Bosons (e.g., photons, helium-4 atoms) have integer spin and can occupy the same quantum state in unlimited numbers, governed by Bose-Einstein statistics rather than the Pauli exclusion principle.

questions.question: Fermi-Dirac statistics applies to particles known as fermions, which
options: Have half-integer spin and obey the Pauli exclusion principle, so no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state
Have integer spin and can occupy the same state without limit
Never interact with electromagnetic fields
Always have zero rest mass
questions.correct_answer: Have half-integer spin and obey the Pauli exclusion principle, so no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state
questions.explanation: Fermions (e.g., electrons, protons, neutrons) have half-integer spin and are restricted by the Pauli exclusion principle, which shapes the Fermi-Dirac distribution used to describe their statistical occupation of energy states.

questions.question: The Bose-Einstein distribution function giving the average occupation number of a single-particle state with energy epsilon is
options: n(epsilon) = 1 / (exp((epsilon-mu)/(k_B*T)) - 1)
n(epsilon) = 1 / (exp((epsilon-mu)/(k_B*T)) + 1)
n(epsilon) = exp(-(epsilon-mu)/(k_B*T))
n(epsilon) = (epsilon - mu) / (k_B*T)
questions.correct_answer: n(epsilon) = 1 / (exp((epsilon-mu)/(k_B*T)) - 1)
questions.explanation: The Bose-Einstein distribution has a minus sign in the denominator, distinguishing it from Fermi-Dirac (plus sign); mu is the chemical potential, and the distribution allows unlimited occupation of a state as epsilon approaches mu.

questions.question: The Fermi-Dirac distribution function giving the average occupation number of a single-particle state with energy epsilon is
options: n(epsilon) = 1 / (exp((epsilon-mu)/(k_B*T)) + 1)
n(epsilon) = 1 / (exp((epsilon-mu)/(k_B*T)) - 1)
n(epsilon) = exp(-(epsilon-mu)/(k_B*T))
n(epsilon) = mu / epsilon
questions.correct_answer: n(epsilon) = 1 / (exp((epsilon-mu)/(k_B*T)) + 1)
questions.explanation: The plus sign in the denominator ensures the Fermi-Dirac occupation number never exceeds 1, consistent with the Pauli exclusion principle limiting each state to at most one fermion.

questions.question: In the classical (Maxwell-Boltzmann) limit, both the Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac distributions reduce to the Boltzmann distribution when
options: The average occupation number per state is much less than 1 (low density or high temperature, so quantum degeneracy effects become negligible)
The temperature approaches absolute zero
The particles have exactly zero energy
The chemical potential mu is much greater than the particle energy epsilon
questions.correct_answer: The average occupation number per state is much less than 1 (low density or high temperature, so quantum degeneracy effects become negligible)
questions.explanation: When exp((epsilon-mu)/k_BT) is much greater than 1, the +/-1 term in the denominator of both quantum distributions becomes negligible, and both reduce to the classical Boltzmann exponential form.

questions.question: At absolute zero temperature, a system of fermions fills all available single-particle states up to a maximum energy known as the
options: Fermi energy
Boltzmann energy
Zero-point energy of the harmonic oscillator
Rydberg energy
questions.correct_answer: Fermi energy
questions.explanation: At T=0, the Pauli exclusion principle forces fermions to fill the lowest available energy states one by one, up to the Fermi energy, above which all states are empty.

questions.question: The classical Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics differs from both quantum statistics (Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac) in that it
options: Treats identical particles as distinguishable and imposes no restriction on the number of particles per state
Applies the Pauli exclusion principle strictly to all particles
Allows only bosonic particles to be described
Predicts identical distributions to Fermi-Dirac statistics at all temperatures
questions.correct_answer: Treats identical particles as distinguishable and imposes no restriction on the number of particles per state
questions.explanation: Classical statistics ignores quantum indistinguishability and exclusion effects, treating particles as labelable and allowing any occupation number per state, which is only a good approximation when quantum degeneracy is negligible.

questions.question: Deriving the ideal gas law PV = Nk_BT from statistical mechanics typically starts from
options: The classical canonical partition function of N non-interacting particles in a box, using the Maxwell-Boltzmann (classical) approximation
The Fermi-Dirac distribution at absolute zero only
The Bose-Einstein condensation temperature formula
The Planck blackbody radiation formula directly
questions.correct_answer: The classical canonical partition function of N non-interacting particles in a box, using the Maxwell-Boltzmann (classical) approximation
questions.explanation: The ideal gas law emerges naturally from computing the partition function for N independent classical particles confined to a volume V and using thermodynamic relations (P = -dF/dV) to obtain the equation of state.

questions.question: The Einstein model of the specific heat of solids treats each atom in the crystal lattice as
options: An independent quantum harmonic oscillator, all vibrating at the same fixed frequency
A free classical particle with no restoring force
A fermion obeying the Pauli exclusion principle
A photon in a cavity
questions.correct_answer: An independent quantum harmonic oscillator, all vibrating at the same fixed frequency
questions.explanation: Einstein modeled solid-state vibrations as 3N independent quantum harmonic oscillators of a single frequency, successfully explaining the qualitative drop in specific heat at low temperatures (unlike the classical Dulong-Petit prediction).

questions.question: The classical Dulong-Petit law predicts that the molar specific heat of a solid at high temperature approaches
options: 3R (where R is the universal gas constant)
questions.correct_answer: 3R (where R is the universal gas constant)
questions.explanation: Classical equipartition of energy assigns (1/2)k_BT to each of the 6 quadratic degrees of freedom (3 kinetic + 3 potential) per atom in a lattice, giving a molar specific heat of 3R, which matches experiment at high temperature.

questions.question: At low temperatures, the Einstein model correctly predicts that the specific heat of a solid
options: Decreases toward zero as temperature decreases, unlike the constant 3R predicted classically
Remains exactly constant at 3R at all temperatures
Increases without bound as temperature decreases
Becomes negative
questions.correct_answer: Decreases toward zero as temperature decreases, unlike the constant 3R predicted classically
questions.explanation: Because vibrational energy levels are quantized (hbar*omega spacing), at low temperature most oscillators freeze into their ground state and cannot absorb thermal energy in small increments, so the specific heat drops toward zero, a key success of quantum statistical mechanics over the classical Dulong-Petit law.

questions.question: Blackbody radiation is successfully explained using Bose-Einstein statistics because photons
options: Are bosons with zero chemical potential (since photon number is not conserved), allowing derivation of the Planck spectral distribution
Are fermions that obey the Pauli exclusion principle
Have half-integer spin
Can only exist in a single quantum state at a given temperature
questions.correct_answer: Are bosons with zero chemical potential (since photon number is not conserved), allowing derivation of the Planck spectral distribution
questions.explanation: Treating the photon gas in a cavity using Bose-Einstein statistics, with chemical potential set to zero because photons can be freely created and absorbed, reproduces Planck's blackbody radiation law.

questions.question: Planck's law for the spectral energy density of blackbody radiation, derived using Bose-Einstein statistics, correctly predicts that at high frequencies the spectrum
options: Falls off exponentially, avoiding the 'ultraviolet catastrophe' predicted by classical physics
Diverges to infinity, consistent with classical Rayleigh-Jeans predictions
Is independent of frequency entirely
Only applies to frequencies below the visible spectrum
questions.correct_answer: Falls off exponentially, avoiding the 'ultraviolet catastrophe' predicted by classical physics
questions.explanation: Planck's quantization of radiation energy introduces an exponential suppression factor at high frequency, correcting the classical Rayleigh-Jeans law which incorrectly diverged (the ultraviolet catastrophe).

questions.question: The Stefan-Boltzmann law, which states that the total power radiated per unit area by a blackbody is proportional to T^4, can be derived by
options: Integrating the Planck spectral distribution over all frequencies
Applying the classical equipartition theorem alone
Using only the Fermi-Dirac distribution
Assuming radiation has zero energy at all temperatures
questions.correct_answer: Integrating the Planck spectral distribution over all frequencies
questions.explanation: Integrating the Bose-Einstein-derived Planck spectral energy density over all frequencies yields the total radiated energy density, which is proportional to T^4, recovering the empirically known Stefan-Boltzmann law.

questions.question: A key qualitative difference between the specific heat of a classical ideal gas and a system of electrons in a metal (Fermi gas) at ordinary temperatures is that
options: The electronic contribution to specific heat is strongly suppressed because only electrons near the Fermi energy can be thermally excited, due to the Pauli exclusion principle
Electrons contribute exactly the same specific heat as predicted by classical equipartition
Electrons in metals do not obey any exclusion principle
The Fermi gas specific heat is always larger than the classical gas prediction
questions.correct_answer: The electronic contribution to specific heat is strongly suppressed because only electrons near the Fermi energy can be thermally excited, due to the Pauli exclusion principle
questions.explanation: Because most electrons in a degenerate Fermi gas are already in filled states, only those within roughly k_BT of the Fermi energy can absorb thermal energy, drastically reducing the electronic specific heat compared to the classical equipartition prediction.

questions.question: In statistical mechanics, the term 'ensemble' refers to
options: A large (conceptually infinite) collection of virtual copies of a system, each representing a possible microstate consistent with given macroscopic constraints
A single, specific microstate of one physical system
The collection of all possible macroscopic measuring instruments
A term used only in quantum statistics, not classical
questions.correct_answer: A large (conceptually infinite) collection of virtual copies of a system, each representing a possible microstate consistent with given macroscopic constraints
questions.explanation: An ensemble is a statistical (mental) construct: many copies of the system, distributed over its accessible microstates, used to compute ensemble averages that correspond to measured macroscopic quantities.

questions.question: The grand canonical ensemble differs from the canonical ensemble in that it allows a system to exchange
options: Both energy and particles with a reservoir, at fixed chemical potential mu and temperature T
Only volume, but not energy or particles
Neither energy nor particles with any reservoir
Only particles, but never any energy
questions.correct_answer: Both energy and particles with a reservoir, at fixed chemical potential mu and temperature T
questions.explanation: The grand canonical ensemble generalizes the canonical ensemble by also allowing particle exchange, introducing the chemical potential mu as the variable conjugate to particle number; it is the natural ensemble for deriving Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac statistics.

questions.question: For an ideal gas of N molecules in the classical (Maxwell-Boltzmann) regime, the total partition function Z_N for indistinguishable particles is related to the single-particle partition function z by
options: Z_N = z^N / N!
Z_N = N * z
Z_N = z^N
Z_N = z / N
questions.correct_answer: Z_N = z^N / N!
questions.explanation: The factor of N! corrects for overcounting configurations that differ only by permuting identical, indistinguishable particles; omitting it leads to the unphysical Gibbs paradox in entropy calculations.
